claims.text: Nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles can serve as noble-metal-based HEA precursors.
The AuCoCuNiPt precursor nanoparticles are uniformly mixed.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles undergo pronounced atomic diffusion and temperature-dependent structural and chemical evolution.
Advanced free-energy sampling can map selective dealloying pathways in noble-metal-based HEA precursors.
Free-energy-guided selective dealloying will enable formation of three-dimensional HEA nanoframeworks with precise atomic control.
Dealloying conditions can be selected from a free-energy landscape generated by metadynamics.
Adjusting pH, electrochemical potential, and temperature permits selective dissolution of less noble elements while retaining an overall high-entropy composition.
Selective removal of labile metal species produces a porous, interconnected three-dimensional framework enriched in noble, corrosion-resistant metals.
Metadynamics or umbrella sampling can map intermediate-state energetics during dealloying.
The mapped free-energy landscape permits precise tuning of element-specific dissolution kinetics.
Controlled element removal yields a high-surface-area interconnected framework while preserving atomic-level high-entropy characteristics.
The resulting nanoframework will have greater porosity and surface area than conventionally synthesized HEAs.
Preserved atomic-level mixing and increased surface area will enhance catalytic properties.

Conventional synthesis, including pulsed laser deposition without guided dealloying, typically produces agglomerated nanoparticles or phase-separated structures with limited three-dimensional structural control.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles can form an AuCu surface layer and undergo phase separation at elevated temperature.
Successful framework formation is confined to a chemical-potential window defined by pH, temperature, and applied potential.
Excessively rapid dealloying may cause structural collapse, whereas insufficient dealloying may leave framework formation incomplete.
A comparison of free-energy-optimized dealloying against conventional dealloying can test whether optimization improves framework uniformity, porosity, or catalytic performance.
